newsitem.title: USA: Germans gain on Saturn in J.D. Power sales survey.
newsitem.headline: Germans gain on Saturn in J.D. Power sales survey.

text.p: Saturn dealers maintained their lead in providing the most satisfying car-buying experience, but top German luxury makes are quickly gaining ground, according to a new J.D. Power & Associates consumer survey.
Mercedes-Benz, Porsche AG and Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG moved into the second, third and fourth-place spots in Power's Sales Satisfaction Study, released Wednesday.

The German automakers' U.S. dealer networks vaulted ahead of Japanese luxury makes, including Lexus, which has tied or tailgated Saturn since 1995 in the poll of 45,000 Americans who bought new cars and trucks in November and December 1996.

"Where they seem to have made their strides is in the sales person performance, particularly in communication," said Loretta Seymour, J.D. Power's director of automotive sales research. "They have put some focused effort and training in this whole area."

Saturn, the upstart General Motors Corp. small car unit that revolutionised the sales process seven years ago with no-haggle pricing and low-pressure, salaried sales associates, led the industry with a survey score of 157 out of 160, three points higher than last year.

Mercedes, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, moved up from fifth to second with a score of 156, while Porsche moved from ninth to third, with 156. BMW moved up five spots to tie Toyota Motor Corp.'s Lexus and AB Volvo at 153. Lexus tied with Saturn for first place last year.
Rounding out the top 10 were Volkswagen AG's Audi unit, 152; Ford Motor Co.'s Jaguar unit, 151; BMW's Land Rover unit, 151; and GM's Cadillac and Nissan Motor Co. Ltd's Infiniti, both with 150.

Finishing below the industry average score of 128 were, in alphabetical order, Chrysler, Dodge, Eagle, Honda, Hyundai, Isuzu, Jeep, Kia, Mazda, Mitsubishi, Nissan, Plymouth, Pontiac, Subaru, Suzuki and Toyota.

The average improved significantly from the 1996 score of 119, which had dropped from 122 in 1995, marking the first-ever decline in the survey since it was started in 1987. Seymour attributed the improvement partly to consumers being more satisfied with the leasing process.

The leaders' performances excelled in the areas of salesperson communication, the convenience of the transaction process and buyers' confidence in vehicle quality. Power said automakers that have been able to speed the sales process along and offer a more relaxed negotiation process are improving the most.

"Customers are looking for guidance from their salesperson rather than a time-consuming deal," Seymour said. "To continue to increase sales satisfaction, the industry must continue to focus on customer communication and its role in making the entire purchase process easier."
